body:
Storing lower/upper bounds might significantly increase the size of metadata for datasets with a big number of columns, which can degrade the performance of metadata operations. In most cases, users cluster/sort their data by a subset of data columns to have fast queries with predicates on those columns. In my view, it is reasonable to have a list of columns for which we want to collect stats and that should be configurable by the user.
Another option here is to add a flag to keep stats only for top-level columns. I believe the first approach is more flexible and will help us to properly support nested datasets. This will be really beneficial in light of upcoming changes for nested data in Spark.
This feature should coexist with #113.
title: Make collection of lower/upper bounds configurable

body:
Users should be able to use Iceberg tables as sinks for Spark structured streaming.
Spark provides queryId and epochId to all sinks, which must ensure that all writes are idempotent. Spark might try to commit the same batch multiple times. So, we need to know the latest committed epochId for every query. One way to do so is by persisting queryId and epochId in the snapshot summary. On writes, we can simply iterate through the snapshots and check the latest committed epochId for a given query to make writes idempotent.
title: Use Iceberg tables as sinks for Spark Structured Streaming

body:
Based on the discussion on dev mailing list:
Ryan Blue

So far, we’ve kept these around to help troubleshoot format problems. It has been a fairly cheap way to be able to see exactly what happened to the table. But we’re also getting to the point where we no longer need to refer back to them and should think about adding a way to remove them. Technically, you don’t need to keep them around once you’ve committed the new version, but an easy way to roll back is to change the database pointer so it is nice to keep a few of them.
I think we can probably build a way to expire old metadata versions by looking for a naming pattern, like v(num)-(uuid).metadata.json[.gz].
title: Add mechanism to expire old metadata versions

body:
I was writing a test case for #132 and noticed the code path here looks like it's expecting the values to be read via Configuration as bootstrapped from Iceberg to Parquet names here but digging into this it ends up instantiating a ParquetWriter that is expecting that rowGroupSize and ParquetProperties were configured explicitly instead of reading via key/values in the configuration. This made it so I couldn't generate a file via the iceberg Parquet API with multiple row groups by artificially reducing the row group size for the test.
Also, I'm not sure the other branch here ends up respecting the other properties such as dictionary and page size (I couldn't find where they were configured at least) - rowGroupSize is set explicitly though in that case. In that code path Iceberg's own ParquetWriter is used which delegates to a Parquet's ParquetFileWriter but I don't see where page/dictionary size is configured in that case. In comparison the other code path has InternalParquetRecordWriter --> ParquetFileWriter where InternalParquetRecordWriter has a ParquetProperties which is used to instantiate the ColumnWriteStore which considers page size. The dictionary size used appears to just get the default value from the properties constructed here. Also those properties are making the Parquet format version always hardcoded as V1, not sure if that is intended?
title: Parquet writer doesn't consider configuration properties in some cases (rowGroupSize, pageSize, dictionarySize)

body:
In  SparkOrcReader#read we build a DAG of converters everytime we  call the read method.  This  DAG converts an ORC row to Spark InternalRow. This seems like an expensive operation as it traverse the whole row structure. It seems that building of the converters can be taken out of the read method, and done only once. Ideally all it should require is the structure of the row (schema) to figure how how it will convert an ORC row to InternalRow.
@edgarRd do you think this makes sense? I have a rough idea in my mind on how to implement it.  But let me know if you think this could not be possible.
title: `SparkOrcReader#read()` can potentially be optimized
